claims.text: Settlement patterns come in three shapes: dispersed, with buildings spread out across the land; nucleated, with buildings clustered round a centre such as a well, a church or a market square; and linear, with buildings strung along a line such as a road, a river bank or a valley floor. The test of the pattern is the shape the buildings make on the map, not their number.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Each pattern forms because of what the land and the livelihood ask of the people: nucleation suits a place where one point holds what everyone needs; dispersion suits farming where each family works its own land and the homestead stands on it; linear settlement appears where a line, a road, a river or a valley floor, supplies water, flat land and transport at once.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the dry lands of Namibia settlement clusters at water: thin ribbons of settlement follow the ephemeral rivers such as the Kuiseb and the Swakop, while the commercial farms of the central plateau carry a dispersed pattern because each homestead stands on its own large farm, kilometres from its neighbours.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Site is the land a settlement is built on and its physical features, its water supply, its relief, its soil, its building materials and, historically, its defensive value; situation is the settlement's position relative to the area around it, its routes, its neighbouring settlements and the resources within reach; function is what the settlement does now, and a town can change its function while its site stays fixed.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A good site solved the problems of daily life: reliable water, because every household and its livestock drink daily; flat or gently sloping ground, because building on it is cheap; fertile soil; building materials within reach; and, in older centuries, defensible ground. Where water was scarce the wet-point site beside a spring or river won; where floods were the danger the dry-point site above the flood line won.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Growth follows the situation: settlements grow where their position lets them serve routes and resources, at a ford or bridge, at a harbour, at a road junction, beside a mine or in a capital where administration gathers work, and because situations change, functions change too, so a market town can become a commuter dormitory and a port left behind by bigger ships can decline.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Windhoek began at the hot springs in the valley the Nama called Ai-Gams: its site offered water in a semi-arid land on a level plateau basin at about 1 650 metres above sea level, and its situation, near the crossing of the routes between the north and the south, made it the seat of the colonial administration in 1890 and, from 1990, the capital of independent Namibia, now home to around 486 000 people (2023).

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A settlement hierarchy ranks settlements by the number and order of their services, from hamlet to city; each service needs a threshold population, the smallest number of people needed to keep it in business, and serves a sphere of influence, the area people travel from to use it; low-order services are used often and need small thresholds, while high-order services such as hospitals and universities need large ones, which is why they sit in the largest settlements.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Namibia shows the hierarchy plainly: Windhoek, about 486 000 people (2023), holds the country's main hospital, its university and its international airport; Oshakati, about 59 000 people (2023), holds an intermediate hospital and a large open market; and the small settlements of the communal lands hold a primary school, a clinic and a shop or two, so people travel up the hierarchy for high-order services.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The hierarchy ranks settlements by the number and order of their services, not by physical size or population alone, and a good is something bought and carried away, such as bread or a blanket, whereas a service is work done for the customer, such as teaching, medical care or hair cutting; the test of a ranking is whether it counts services.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Oshana region of northern Namibia holds three fast-growing towns within about 30 kilometres of each other, Oshakati with about 59 000 people (2023), Ongwediva with about 34 000 and Ondangwa with about 30 000, amid one of the densest farmed landscapes in the country, a rural population of about 230 000 (2023) whose homesteads and fields fill the ground between the towns.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the Oshana corridor the highest-order services concentrate where the threshold populations are: only Oshakati holds the intermediate hospital and the region's large open market, only Ondangwa holds the airport, while the surrounding villages keep a clinic, a primary school and small shops, which means villagers travel to the towns for services above the village threshold.
